grammar.title: Passive voice: be + past participle
grammar.explanation_pt:
Na **voz ativa**, o foco está em **quem faz**: "Oscar Niemeyer **designed** Brasília."
Na **voz passiva**, o foco está **no que aconteceu** ou **no objeto**: "Brasília **was designed** by Oscar Niemeyer."

**Estrutura:** sujeito + **be** (no tempo certo) + **particípio passado** (+ by + agente)

- **Present simple passive:** am / is / are + particípio → "Coffee **is grown** in Brazil." / "These phones **are made** in China."
- **Past simple passive:** was / were + particípio → "The Eiffel Tower **was built** in 1889." / "The windows **were broken**."

**Negativa e pergunta:** mexa só no **be**: "It **wasn't made** in Italy." / "**Where was** it **made**?" / "**When were** the pyramids **built**?"

**Quando usar a passiva?**
1. Quando **não sabemos** quem fez: "My bike **was stolen**."
2. Quando **não importa** quem fez: "The office **is cleaned** every night."
3. Quando o **óbvio**: "He **was arrested**." (pela polícia, claro)
4. Em textos **formais, científicos e notícias**.

**By + agente** só quando a informação é importante: "*Dom Casmurro* **was written by** Machado de Assis."

rows: They make these shoes in Franca.
These shoes are made in Franca.
The 14-bis was flown by Santos Dumont in 1906.

grammar.tip_pt: Para a passiva funcionar, você precisa dominar os **particípios** (built, made, written, sold, spoken, grown, stolen, chosen). Revise a lista de verbos irregulares!

common_mistakes.why_pt: A passiva precisa do verbo be.

listening.title: Podcast: everyday inventions

lines.speaker: Host
lines.en: Did you know that many everyday objects were invented by accident? Post-it notes were created when a scientist was trying to make a strong glue — and failed. reading.title: The story of coffee
reading.text: Coffee is drunk by billions of people every day, but where did it come from? According to legend, coffee was discovered in Ethiopia, when a goat herder noticed that his goats became very energetic after eating some red berries. The plant was later taken to Yemen, where coffee was first prepared as a drink. In the 18th century, coffee seeds were brought to Brazil — legend says they were secretly given to a Portuguese officer in French Guiana. Today, Brazil is the world's largest coffee producer: around a third of the world's coffee is grown here, mainly in Minas Gerais, São Paulo and Espírito Santo. The beans are harvested between May and September and are exported to more than 100 countries.

questions.answer: In Ethiopia.

lessons.title: Breaking news
lessons.subtitle_pt: Past perfect: o passado do passado
objectives: Mostrar que uma ação aconteceu antes de outra no passado

warmup.text_pt: "Quando cheguei ao cinema, o filme **já tinha começado**." Esse "já tinha começado" é o **past perfect**: uma ação passada que aconteceu **antes** de outra ação passada.

grammar.title: Past perfect
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Estrutura:** **had** + particípio passado (igual para todas as pessoas)
- Afirmativa: I **had** (I'd) **finished**. / She'd **left**.
- Negativa: They **hadn't seen** it.
- Pergunta: **Had** you **been** there before?

**Uso:** mostrar que uma ação aconteceu **antes** de outra ação **no passado**. É o "tinha feito".

Linha do tempo:
[ação 1 — past perfect] → [ação 2 — simple past] → agora
"When I **got** to the station, the train **had left**." (o trem saiu primeiro; depois eu cheguei)

Compare:
- "When I arrived, the train **left**." = cheguei e então o trem saiu (vi saindo)
- "When I arrived, the train **had left**." = o trem saiu antes de eu chegar (perdi!)

**Palavras frequentes:** **by the time**, **when**, **already**, **just**, **never... before**, **before**, **after**, **because**.

**Já com before e after**, a ordem fica clara e o past perfect é opcional: "After I (had) finished, I went home."

💡 Em notícias e histórias, o past perfect volta no tempo para explicar o contexto: "The firefighters rescued a man who **had been** trapped for six hours."

examples.en: By the time the firefighters arrived, the neighbors had already rescued the dog.
examples.pt: Quando os bombeiros chegaram, os vizinhos já tinham resgatado o cachorro.

examples.en: I'd never seen snow before I moved to Canada.
examples.pt: Eu nunca tinha visto neve antes de me mudar para o Canadá.

examples.en: It turned out that the man had lost his memory after the accident.
examples.pt: Descobriu-se que o homem tinha perdido a memória depois do acidente.

grammar.tip_pt: Cuidado com a contração **'d**: pode ser **had** ("I'd finished") ou **would** ("I'd go"). Se vem particípio depois, é **had**; se vem verbo base, é **would**.

common_mistakes.wrong: When I arrived, the party already finished.
common_mistakes.right: When I arrived, the party had already finished.
common_mistakes.why_pt: A festa terminou antes da chegada: past perfect.

common_mistakes.wrong: I had saw that movie before.
common_mistakes.right: I had seen that movie before.

common_mistakes.wrong: I had went to bed when you called.
common_mistakes.right: I had gone to bed when you called.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Na fala, **had** quase sempre vira **'d**, que é muito curto: "I'd left" = "áid léft", "she'd gone" = "shíd gón". Às vezes o 'd é quase inaudível — o particípio é o que mostra que é past perfect.

reading.title: The wallet that came back
reading.text: Last month, a taxi driver in Belo Horizonte made headlines for an act of honesty. Carlos Mendes, 54, had just finished his shift when he noticed a wallet on the back seat. A passenger had dropped it earlier that day. Inside, there was 3,000 reais in cash, credit cards and a plane ticket to Lisbon for the next morning. Carlos didn't have the owner's phone number, but he found a business card in the wallet. He called the number, and it turned out that it belonged to the passenger's daughter. By the time Carlos reached the passenger's house, the man had already canceled his cards and had almost given up on his trip. "I'd never felt so relieved," said the passenger. When he tried to give Carlos a reward, the driver refused. "I only did what anyone should do," he said.

questions.q: What had the passenger done before Carlos arrived?

lessons.title: Storms and floods
objectives: Nomear desastres naturais e fenômenos climáticos
Combinar simple past, past continuous e past perfect numa narrativa
Usar a passiva em relatos de desastres (were evacuated, was destroyed)

warmup.text_pt: O Brasil sofre principalmente com enchentes, deslizamentos e secas. Você já viveu algum evento climático extremo? Como foi?
questions: What natural disasters happen in Brazil?
Are extreme weather events becoming more common?

chunks.en: It had been raining for days.
We were sleeping when the water came in.
chunks.pt: Estávamos dormindo quando a água entrou.

grammar.title: Tempos narrativos combinados
grammar.explanation_pt:
Para contar um evento passado de forma completa, combine **quatro** estruturas:

1. **Past continuous** → o **cenário**, o que estava acontecendo:
"It **was raining** heavily, and most people **were sleeping**."

2. **Past perfect** → o que tinha acontecido **antes** (contexto, causas):
"It **had been raining** for three days, and the river **had risen** two meters." (had been + -ing = past perfect continuous, para duração antes de um ponto do passado)

3. **Simple past** → os **eventos principais**, em sequência:
"At 3 a.m., the water **reached** the houses. Families **climbed** onto their roofs."

4. **Past passive** → o que **aconteceu com** pessoas e coisas:
"Thousands of people **were evacuated**, and two bridges **were destroyed**."

**Ordem típica de uma reportagem:** o que aconteceu (simple past/passive) → contexto e causas (past perfect) → detalhes do momento (past continuous) → consequências (passive) → situação atual (present / present perfect).

rows: It had been raining for days.
The water has gone down. Families need help.

examples.en: In May 2024, after it had been raining for weeks, large areas of Rio Grande do Sul were flooded.
examples.pt: Em maio de 2024, depois de semanas de chuva, grandes áreas do Rio Grande do Sul foram inundadas.

examples.en: We were having dinner when we heard the alarm.
examples.pt: Estávamos jantando quando ouvimos o alarme.

examples.en: Thousands of volunteers came from all over the country, and tons of donations were sent.
examples.pt: Milhares de voluntários vieram de todo o país, e toneladas de doações foram enviadas.

grammar.tip_pt: **Past perfect continuous** (had been + -ing) é o "primo" do present perfect continuous, só que no passado: "It **had been raining** for days **when** the dam broke." (Estava chovendo havia dias quando a barragem rompeu.)

common_mistakes.wrong: Many houses destroyed by the flood.
common_mistakes.right: Many houses were destroyed by the flood.
common_mistakes.why_pt: A passiva precisa do verbo be.

common_mistakes.wrong: We slept when the earthquake started.
common_mistakes.right: We were sleeping when the earthquake started.

common_mistakes.wrong: It rained for three days when the river overflowed.
common_mistakes.right: It had been raining for three days when the river overflowed.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Duração antes de outro ponto do passado = past perfect continuous.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Palavras traiçoeiras: **drought** = "dráut" (rima com out, o GH é mudo). **Flood** = "flâd" (rima com mud, não "flúd"!). **Hurricane** = "RÂ-ri-kein" (EUA). **Earthquake** = "ÂRθ-kuêik".

dialogue.title: The night of the flood
dialogue.context_pt: Um morador de Porto Alegre conta para uma jornalista estrangeira o que viveu na enchente.

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: Can you tell me what happened that night?

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.en: It had been raining for almost a week. We had heard warnings, but nobody expected it to be so bad.

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: Where were you when the water came?
lines.pt: Onde você estava quando a água veio?

reading.title: Climate change and extreme weather
reading.text: Scientists have been warning us for decades: as the planet gets warmer, extreme weather events become more frequent and more intense. In recent years, the world has seen record-breaking heatwaves in Europe, devastating wildfires in Canada and Australia, and severe floods in Pakistan and southern Brazil. Warmer air can hold more water, which means heavier rain when storms happen. At the same time, some regions are suffering from longer droughts. In 2023 and 2024, parts of the Amazon experienced one of the worst droughts on record: rivers dropped to historic lows, and entire communities were left isolated because boats couldn't travel. Experts say that we need two kinds of action: reducing greenhouse gas emissions and adapting our cities — with better drainage, early-warning systems and protected green areas.

questions.answer: Because warmer air can hold more water.

questions.q: What two kinds of action do experts recommend?
questions.answer: Reducing emissions and adapting cities.

grammar.title: Certeza, dúvida e a passiva de relato
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Expressar graus de certeza:**
- Certeza alta: "I'm **sure / certain** that..." / "It's **definitely** true." / "There's **no doubt** that..."
- Probabilidade: "It's **likely / probably** true." / "It **seems / appears that**..."
- Dúvida: "I **doubt** (that)..." / "I'm **not sure / not convinced** that..." / "It's **unlikely** that..."
- Ceticismo: "I find that **hard to believe**." / "That **sounds** too good to be true."

**Passiva de relato (reporting passive)** — muito usada em notícias quando a informação **não é confirmada** ou a fonte é geral:
- **It is said that** + frase → "It is said that the city was founded by pirates."
- **It is believed that** + frase → "It is believed that 30% of online reviews are fake."
- **It is reported / thought / estimated that**...

Outra forma: **sujeito + is said / believed + to + verbo** → "The singer **is said to be** very shy." / "The painting **is believed to be** worth millions."

**Atribuir a fonte:** **According to** + fonte ("According to the WHO...") / "**The report says / claims that**..."

💡 **Claim** = afirmar (sem prova) — sinal de cautela: "The post **claims** that coffee cures cancer."

pronunciation.tip_pt: **Doubt** = "dáut" — o B é mudo (como em debt e subtle)! **Debunk** = "di-BÂNK". **Evidence** = "É-vi-dens" (força no começo). **Biased** = "BÁI-ast".

listening.title: How to spot fake news
listening.context_pt: Uma jornalista dá dicas para identificar notícias falsas em um vídeo educativo.

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: Here are five quick ways to spot fake news. One: check the source. Is it a website you know? Two: read beyond the headline — clickbait headlines are designed to make you angry or scared. Three: check the date — old stories are often shared as if they were new. Four: look for evidence. Are there names, data, links to studies? Five: if it seems too good, or too terrible, to be true, it probably is. And remember: it's believed that people are more likely to share news that confirms what they already think. So be extra careful with stories you love!

reading.title: Lies travel fast
reading.text: "A lie can travel halfway around the world while the truth is putting on its shoes." This famous quote — which, ironically, is often wrongly attributed to Mark Twain — describes a real phenomenon. A well-known study by researchers at MIT analyzed more than 100,000 stories shared on Twitter between 2006 and 2017. It was found that false stories were much more likely to be retweeted than true ones and reached people significantly faster. Why? The researchers believe that fake news is usually more surprising and emotional, and people love sharing things that are new and shocking. Interestingly, the study suggested that humans, not bots, were mainly responsible for the spread. With AI tools now able to create realistic fake images and videos, experts say media literacy — the ability to evaluate information critically — is one of the most important skills of the 21st century.

writing.model:
How to spot fake news on WhatsApp 📱

It is estimated that millions of fake messages are shared in Brazil every day, so here are some simple tips. First, check the source: if the message says "a doctor friend said" but there's no name, I doubt it's reliable. Second, look at the date — many stories are years old. Third, be careful with messages that make you very angry or scared: they're often designed to go viral. If something seems too good (or too terrible) to be true, it probably is. Before forwarding, search for the story on a fact-checking site like Aos Fatos or Lupa. According to these sites, health and politics are the most common topics of fake news. And remember: if you're not sure, don't share!

culture_note.title: Checagem de fatos
culture_note.text_pt: Agências de **fact-checking** como Snopes (EUA), Full Fact (Reino Unido) e, no Brasil, Lupa e Aos Fatos verificam boatos virais. Em inglês, quando algo é desmentido, se diz que foi **debunked**; quando é confirmado, **verified**.
